newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle snares Hubble telescope for refit.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle snares Hubble telescope for refit.

text.p: The space shuttle Discovery's robot arm reached out on Thursday and gently snared the Hubble Space Telescope in preparation for a $350 million refurbishment.

The 50-ft (15-metre)-long robot arm, operated by astronaut Steve Hawley, captured the gleaming 12-tonne observatory at 3:33 a.m. EST (0833 GMT) as the two craft soared 360 miles (575 km) above the Pacific Ocean, southwest of Mexico.
Hawley, an astrophysicist and astronomer who rejoined NASA's astronaut corps for this mission, was involved in launching the telescope during a 1990 shuttle mission.
"I wish you could see the expression on Dr. Stevie's face," shuttle commander Ken Bowersox radioed mission control. "Looks like he just shook hands with an old friend."

"Congratulations to all of you for an outstanding rendezvous and a great capture," mission control's Marc Garneau replied. "We're looking forward to getting out there and starting to work on that telescope."

The telescope was gently lowered onto a servicing platform in the rear of the shuttle's cargo bay. The successful capture came after Bowersox and copilot Scott Horowitz had manoeuvred Discovery 35 feet (11 metres) below Hubble, bringing it within reach of the arm.
The smooth rendezvous also means Discovery probably has enough rocket fuel to raise the telescope's orbit by 3 to 4 miles (5-6.5 km) and prolong its lifetime, flight director Jeff Bantle said.

The first of the mission's four spacewalks to upgrade the observatory was scheduled to start as early as 10:30 p.m. EST (0330 GMT) on Thursday. During a six-hour excursion, astronauts Mark Lee and Steve Smith were to install two improved scientific instruments, each about the size of a large refrigerator, in the telescope.

A $105 million multipurpose infrared camera will allow astronomers to see deeper into the universe and may discover planets orbiting other stars, while a $125 million improved spectrograph will help in the search for massive black holes devouring stars in the centre of galaxies.

Upgrades planned over the following three days include the installation of a new digital tape recorder, a more accurate guidance sensor for pointing the telescope and various improved electronic boxes.

The refurbishment work will be complicated by the telescope's fragile 40-ft (13-metre) long solar arrays. The astronauts planned to take great care not to upset the delicate structures, which provide the telescope's power.

The twin solar wings appeared to be warped in television pictures beamed back during the shuttle's final approach but no more than expected, officials said. "The arrays look like they're in pretty darn good shape," astronaut Greg Harbaugh radioed mission control.

The telescope showed some signs of wear and tear after nearly seven years in space. Parts of a NASA logo had peeled off and a piece of space debris appeared to have punched a small hole through an antenna dish.

It was the first time astronauts had visited the $2 billion orbiting observatory since the 1993 repair mission that fixed its blurred vision. Since that mission, the Hubble telescope has provided scientists with the first conclusive evidence of the existence of huge black holes and the discovery of planetary nurseries around stars.
The telescope has also collected light emission data from distant galaxies and other evidence that the universe may be much younger than previously thought.
